headline: High risk of data leakage and capability conflict: Open Interpreter can read/write the local filesystem while EMQX has broad network egress, creating unsafe default pairings.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: No direct shared channel is documented, but Open Interpreter can read clipboard/files and execute shell commands, while EMQX exposes HTTP APIs and broad egress. If EMQX output is manually copied or file-shared into Open Interpreter, prompt injection is possible. The pathway is indirect and requires unusual bridging, so low fits better than medium.
conditions: IF EMQX output is copied into Open Interpreter prompts or files, injected instructions can be executed.
IF a shared clipboard or shared file is used as the bridge, attacker-controlled text can influence Open Interpreter.
mitigations: Disable clipboard-based transfer between the agents.
Use a strict prompt template that strips instructions from imported text.
Review any EMQX-generated text before pasting into Open Interpreter.
Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for all inter-agent content.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Open Interpreter can read the entire user filesystem and handle model provider API keys, while EMQX touches IoT data and has broad network egress. If EMQX outputs or files are fed into Open Interpreter, sensitive local data can be exposed to third-party model providers. The default filesystem access makes the blast radius large and the pathway plausible.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter is run on a machine containing sensitive local files, those files are readable by the agent.
IF Open Interpreter sends context to configured model providers, any imported EMQX data can leave the machine.
mitigations: Run Open Interpreter in a separate user account.
Restrict its filesystem access to a dedicated working directory.
Avoid passing EMQX logs or payloads into Open Interpreter.
Use local-only model providers where possible.
requires-engineering: enforce per-file allowlists and redaction before inference.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: EMQX can make HTTP API calls and has broad network egress, while Open Interpreter can execute shell commands, write the filesystem, and modify git state. If both operate on the same workspace or deployment artifacts, concurrent writes and state changes can collide. The shared filesystem concurrency model on Open Interpreter makes this a default-dangerous overlap.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Open Interpreter modifies git state while EMQX-generated artifacts are being updated, repository corruption or lost changes can occur.
mitigations: Assign separate directories to each agent.
Pause one agent before the other writes shared artifacts.
Use git locks or a single-writer workflow.
Keep EMQX outputs read-only for Open Interpreter.
requires-engineering: add transactional locking around shared state.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Open Interpreter can act on shell and filesystem outputs, so if it consumes EMQX-generated text as authoritative, mistakes can cascade into commands or commits. EMQX itself is not documented as a verifier, so the pair lacks a built-in validation step. The pathway exists in default configurations, but the downstream harm is usually bounded to local actions.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter treats EMQX output as instructions or facts without verification, it may execute incorrect actions.
IF EMQX emits malformed or stale data, Open Interpreter can propagate the error into shell commands or commits.
mitigations: Require human review before execution.
Insert a validation step between EMQX output and Open Interpreter actions.
Use dry-run mode for any shell or git operation.
Limit Open Interpreter to non-destructive commands.
requires-engineering: add schema validation for EMQX-to-automation handoffs.

E_compliance.rationale: EMQX touches IoT data, while Open Interpreter can access anything reachable on the local machine and send context to configured model providers. That creates a plausible residency and retention mismatch if IoT payloads or local regulated data are processed by external model APIs. The profiles do not specify HIPAA/GDPR status, so uncertainty pushes this to medium rather than low.
conditions: IF regulated IoT or personal data is routed from EMQX into Open Interpreter, external model-provider processing may violate policy.
IF the deployment requires strict local-only retention, Open Interpreter's configured providers can create a mismatch.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of Open Interpreter prompts.
Use a local-only model backend.
Redact identifiers before transfer.
Document retention and residency boundaries.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data-class routing.
